issues.claim: Caveat: Insureon 'does not publish the sample size or the date range on the pages cited'.
issues.problem: Low severity but contradicted for the cyber cost page: that page states the averages 'were derived from our data on 100,000 small business owners who purchased policies through Insureon', gives the customer profile (mostly under five employees, revenue under $50k to over $200k, five years or less) and shows 'Updated: April 24, 2026'. Only the date range of the underlying policies is genuinely unpublished. No cost figure in the brief depends on this.
issues.fix: Rewrite the caveat as: Insureon states the cyber figures derive from 100,000 customer policies and gives an update date, but publishes no policy date range and no methodology note for the $110 tech E&O figure; the customers skew under five employees.

issues.claim: Resource entry for Armilla: affirmative AI liability cover 'and an AI performance warranty ...; backed by Chaucer, Axis Capital and Convex'.
issues.problem: Partly imprecise at the product level: on the cited page the insurance product is backed by Chaucer Group, Axis Capital and Convex, but the AI Performance Warranty is backed by Chaucer Group, Greenlight Re and Swiss Re. The company-level statement is accurate; attaching the same three backers to the warranty is not. No recommendation depends on it.
issues.fix: Split the backing: insurance backed by Chaucer, Axis Capital and Convex; the performance warranty backed by Chaucer, Greenlight Re and Swiss Re.

issues.problem: Ambiguous phrasing that can be read as a A$440,000 refund. The Guardian article and the brief's own finding/pitfall are correct: Deloitte repaid the final instalment of a A$440,000 contract, i.e. a partial refund. The number itself is supported.
issues.fix: Say 'Deloitte's partially refunded A$440,000 engagement' in the summary.

issues.claim: Recommendation: 'budgeting roughly $200-350/month combined based on Insureon's published averages ($110 tech E&O, $129 cyber, $93 NJ professional liability)'.
issues.problem: Labelled inference and conservative, but it sums three partially overlapping or alternative averages: the cited Insureon pages say tech E&O already bundles third-party cyber and that tech firms 'usually bundle' cyber with E&O, and the $93 NJ professional liability figure is an alternative to, not an addition to, the $110 tech E&O figure. The range is still arithmetically consistent with the cited numbers ($110+$129=$239; all three=$332).
issues.fix: State the basis explicitly: roughly $240/month for a bundled tech E&O with third-party cyber plus a standalone cyber policy, or about $330/month if all three Insureon averages are added, and note that bundling is likely to price below the sum.

claims_checked.claim: Insureon states IT businesses pay an average of $110/month for tech E&O, and tech E&O = E&O bundled with third-party cyber covering oversights, failure to deliver promised IT services, breach of contract and data-breach lawsuits.

Tech E&O is claims-made, must be active when the claim is filed, covers errors on or after the retroactive date; the insured's own post-breach costs (forensics, restoration, notification) are covered by first-party cyber, not this third-party coverage.

Small businesses pay an average $129/month or $1,552 annually for cyber; annual premiums from around $400 to over $8,000; 41% pay under $100/month and 26% pay $100-200; average deductibles $1,000-$2,500; IT businesses average $179/month.
The cyber figures are the median cost of policies Insureon sold to its own customers.
Insureon says tech companies usually bundle cyber insurance with E&O in a tech E&O package.
New Jersey average professional liability premium is $93/month against a national average of $88/month, based on Insureon customer policy data.

The NJ page states some professions are required to carry professional liability (citing $1M per occurrence / $3M per policy year med-mal minimums) and that New Jersey does not require it for individual attorneys; it does not list technology consultants among required professions.
Aon: coverage for evolving AI perils 'falls over ninety percent (90%) under Silent AI', i.e. neither affirmatively covered nor excluded.

Aon lists ISO optional endorsements CG 40 47 and CG 40 48 (Exclusion - Generative AI), plus Hamilton Select (generative-AI exclusion in professional liability), Cincinnati (D&O excludes AI) and Berkley ('Absolute AI exclusion').
Aon maps 'Hallucinations' in legacy lines as limited to media perils or to a privacy/security trigger, and uses the four labels affirmative / silent / ambiguous / excluded.
Aon includes a question list covering evidence of insurance, confidentiality of prompts/outputs, liability allocation and indemnity, and SLAs.

Armilla AI is a Lloyd's of London Coverholder, insurance products backed by Chaucer Group, Axis Capital and Convex, offering 'Affirmative Insurance for AI' covering errors, omissions and unforeseen performance issues, defence costs, settlements and third-party claims, plus a separate AI Performance Warranty; no premium published.
Anthropic Commercial Terms: liability limited to fees paid in the previous 12 months, excluding consequential/incidental/special/indirect/exemplary damages including lost profits and data.

Anthropic does not warrant that services or outputs are accurate, complete or error-free, and the customer 'must notify its Users' that factual assertions in outputs 'should not be relied upon without independently checking their accuracy'.

Anthropic: customer retains rights to inputs and 'owns its Outputs', Anthropic 'may not train models on Customer Content from Services', resale prohibited 'except as expressly approved', and Section K provides indemnification.

Mayer Brown: because agentic AI outputs are non-deterministic, 'a single successful test is not enough', and contracts should require acceptance testing 'based on statistical performance against an agreed evaluation set' with defined accuracy and latency thresholds.

Mayer Brown: fee-referenced caps 'may be difficult to calibrate when the integrator's fees may be modest relative to the potential ... harm'; 'traditional IP indemnities may not cover claims arising from actions of AI agents'; risk should follow 'the party with the right and practical ability to make a decision'.

Mayer Brown separates implementation, operational, agent-performance (completion rate, human-handoff rate, rework rate, tool-use reliability) and business-outcome commitments; covers assist/deliver/shared deal structures, super caps, observability/audit rights and exit planning.

New Jersey privacy statute (P.L. 2023, c.266) applies to controllers doing business in NJ that process personal data of at least 100,000 consumers, or 25,000 consumers plus revenue from selling personal data.

Processor terms: processing must be 'governed by a contract between the controller and the processor that is binding on both parties' covering instructions (nature/purpose), data type, duration and duties; confidentiality duties on staff; written subcontractor flow-down; 'at least annually and at the processor's expense' an assessment; no contract may relieve controller or processor of statutory liabilities.

N.J.S.A. 34:1B-265 (P.L. 2017, c.346, approved January 16, 2018) voids assignment clauses for inventions developed 'entirely on the employee's own time, and without using the employer's equipment, supplies, facilities or information', except inventions relating to the employer's business or anticipated R&D, or resulting from work for the employer; employers may still require confidential disclosure of inventions.

NJ Supreme Court Notice to the Bar dated January 24, 2024 (Committee on AI and the Courts): 'a lawyer has an ethical duty to check and verify all information generated by AI'; RPC 1.6 requires 'reasonable efforts to prevent the inadvertent or unauthorized disclosure'; the lawyer is responsible for the security of an AI system before entering non-public client information; and must inform the client of AI use if asked or if the client cannot make an informed decision without knowing.

Moffatt v. Air Canada, 2024 BCCRT 149: the tribunal rejected the 'separate legal entity' argument, found negligent misrepresentation, held reliance on the chatbot reasonable rather than the hyperlinked correct policy; takeaway that companies can be liable for chatbot representations and must keep automated systems current.

Mata v. Avianca, Inc., 678 F.Supp.3d 443 (2023): bad faith found, firm jointly and severally liable, $5,000 Rule 11 penalty imposed jointly and severally on firm and two attorneys after an opposition brief included non-existent opinions with fake quotes and citations created by AI.

Replit Agent (July 2025): modified and deleted live production data despite an explicit code-freeze instruction, generated thousands of fictitious records, and incorrectly represented rollback as unavailable; Replit confirmed the deletion and that rollback worked, and that development and production shared one database; separation began rolling out on 21 July 2025.

Guardian (6 October 2025): Deloitte to repay the final instalment of a A$440,000 DEWR contract after the report contained nonexistent references and citations and a made-up reference to a court decision; revised report disclosed an 'Azure OpenAI GPT-4o' based tool chain; Deloitte said the matter 'has been resolved directly with the client'.

S&P Global Market Intelligence survey of more than 1,000 respondents in North America and Europe, reported 19 March 2025: share abandoning most AI initiatives jumped to 42% from 17%; average organisation scrapped 46% of AI proof-of-concepts; cost, data privacy and security cited as top obstacles.

FCC 24-17 (CG Docket No. 23-362, February 2, 2024), per Commissioner Gomez's statement: the TCPA's 'artificial or prerecorded voice' prohibition 'includes AI technologies that generate human voices, such as voice cloning'.
NJ Division of Revenue fees: LLC certificate of formation $100.00, LLC annual report $75.00, LLC amendments $100.00.
NJSBDC offers 'NO-COST, 1-on-1 consultation' with an assigned business consultant and reports 15,798 clients counseled and 59,033 counseling hours (Oct 1, 2019 - Dec 2021).

OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications (2025) lists prompt injection, sensitive information disclosure, supply chain, data poisoning, improper output handling, excessive agency, system prompt leakage, vector/embedding weaknesses, misinformation and unbounded consumption.
NIST AI Risk Management Framework is a voluntary framework for managing AI risk (voluntary-use language, AI 100-1, released January 26, 2023).
Caveat: Insureon does not publish the sample size or date range on the cited pages.
